On March 17, 2026, Oracle released Java 26. And if you work anywhere near enterprise Java, you already know what happened next in most companies.
Absolutely nothing.
Somewhere, an architect glanced at the announcement, saw the words “non-LTS,” and closed the tab. The upgrade ticket stayed in the backlog, right where it’s been since Java 21. Maybe since Java 17. I’ve worked on codebases where it would be since Java 8, and I know I’m not the only one.
I get it. The LTS badge has become the only signal most teams read. But I want to make the case that this reflex is costing you real performance, real security, and a real say in where Java goes next. Because Java 26 is a genuinely good release, and the way we collectively ignore releases like it says something a little broken about how the ecosystem thinks about the six month cadence.
First, a 60 second refresher on how we got here
Since Java 9, Oracle ships a new major version every six months, in March and September. Most of these are “feature releases” supported for exactly six months, until the next one arrives.
